meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice'?
meta.ogDescription: MLK made it famous, but the metaphor is Theodore Parker's 1853 sermon. King quoted the condensed adage in quotation marks from 1958.

answer.label: Not Martin Luther King Jr. — the metaphor is Theodore Parker’s
answer.sourceLine: The idea and imagery come from Parker’s 1853 sermon “Of Justice and the Conscience.” Parker’s own words were long and tentative; the crisp modern wording is a later condensation (documented by 1918). Dr. King quoted this condensed adage — in quotation marks — from 1958 onward and made it famous, but he did not coin it.

source.heading: Where it really comes from

docMeta.dd: “Of Justice and the Conscience,” in Ten Sermons of Religion (1853)
Attested by 1918; popularized by Martin Luther King Jr. from 1958

source.excerpt: I do not pretend to understand the moral universe; the arc is a long one, my eye reaches but little ways; I cannot calculate the curve and complete the figure by the experience of sight; I can divine it by conscience. And from what I see I am sure it bends towards justice.
trail: Theodore Parker gave the metaphor its first form in “Of Justice and the Conscience,” a sermon in his 1853 Ten Sermons of Religion, per Quote Investigator.
The concise modern wording — “The arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice” — was already circulating and credited to Parker by 1918, according to Quote Investigator.

Martin Luther King Jr. used the phrase inside quotation marks — marking it as a pre-existing adage — in his 1958 article “Out of the Long Night,” and repeated it in later speeches, per Quote Investigator.
source.excerptNote: Parker’s original passage from the 1853 sermon — far longer and more hesitant than the aphorism it became.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: full origin of the saying

source.rightsNote: Both Parker’s 1853 sermon and the condensed wording documented by 1918 were published in the United States well before 1931, placing the text in the public domain. (Dr. King’s own later writings remain in copyright, but the wording itself predates and is independent of him.)

author.name: Theodore Parker
author.heading: About Theodore Parker
author.bio: Theodore Parker was a Boston-based Unitarian minister, Transcendentalist, and fierce abolitionist whose sermons influenced a generation of reformers. In an 1853 sermon he reasoned that though we cannot see the whole shape of moral history, conscience assures us it “bends towards justice.” The line was later distilled into the aphorism that Martin Luther King Jr. would make world-famous.

misattribution.heading: How the credit went astray
misattribution.intro: The line is almost universally pinned on Martin Luther King Jr., who quoted it often — but he was passing along a much older idea, and even the famous short wording was not his invention.

items.why: King quoted the adage inside quotation marks as early as his 1958 article “Out of the Long Night,” explicitly signalling it was already in circulation, per Quote Investigator. His frequent, eloquent use is why it is now remembered as “his.”
Parker never wrote the neat one-sentence version; a compressed form was already being credited to him by 1918 in Readings from Great Authors, long before King, per Quote Investigator.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and imagery are Theodore Parker’s (1853); the crisp wording is a later paraphrase; and Dr. King is the man who carried it to the world — a genuine quoter, not the author, as Quote Investigator documents.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The saying became a touchstone of the American civil-rights movement and beyond — carved into the Oval Office rug during the Obama administration and cited in countless speeches. Tracing it back to Theodore Parker doesn’t diminish King; it reveals a chain of moral thought stretching from the abolitionists to the civil-rights era.

Parker’s original was strikingly humble: he admitted he could not see the whole arc and could only “divine it by conscience.” The confident modern aphorism smooths away that uncertainty — a reminder that a memorable line is often a polished descendant of a more tentative original.
context.pull: Parker admitted he could not see the whole arc — only “divine it by conscience.”
